title: Fuzzing
summary: **Fuzzing** feeds a program huge numbers of automatically generated, mostly broken inputs and watches for crashes, hangs and sanitizer reports. Coverage-guided fuzzers such as **libFuzzer** learn which inputs reach new code and mutate those further, finding bugs no human would think to test. This lesson writes fuzz targets for Delve's parsers, runs them with MSVC's fuzzer support and AddressSanitizer, and minimises the crashing inputs.
markdown:
## The idea Tests check the cases you thought of. Bugs live in the cases you did not: a level file with a 2-billion-character line, a save whose length field says 0xFFFFFFFF, a message cut off mid-header. A **fuzzer** generates such inputs automatically, millions per hour: ```mermaid flowchart LR C["Corpus
example inputs"] --> M["Mutate
flip bits, insert, delete,
splice, repeat"] M --> T["Run the fuzz target
with ASan and UBSan"] T -->|"crash or sanitizer report"| R["Save the input as a reproducer"] T -->|"reached new code (coverage)"| C T -->|"nothing new"| M ``` **Coverage guidance** is what makes modern fuzzers effective: the compiler instruments the program to record which code each input reaches, and inputs that reach something new are kept and mutated further. The fuzzer gradually learns the format's structure (the magic number, the version field, valid section headers) without being told. ## Writing a fuzz target A fuzz target is one function that takes a block of bytes and passes them to the code under test: ```cpp-norun // fuzz_level.cpp: fuzz Delve's level parser (lesson 11.02's practice task) #include #include #include #include "level.h" extern "C" int LLVMFuzzerTestOneInput(const uint8_t* data, size_t size) { const std::string text(reinterpret_cast(data), size); const auto level{ parseLevel(text) }; // must never crash, hang or trip a sanitizer if (level) { // Check invariants the parser promises: the result is self-consistent. if (level->tiles.size() != static_cast(level->width * level->height)) __debugbreak(); } return 0; } ``` Good fuzz targets: - **target one parser or decoder** of untrusted data: level files, saves (lessons 10.07, 11.06), INI settings (10.08), telemetry snapshots (12.04), IOCTL request structures (16.05), PE headers (9.02); - are **deterministic** and **fast** (thousands of runs per second); - check **invariants** as well as crashes: a successful parse should produce a consistent result; - do not touch the file system, network or global state. ## Running it with MSVC Visual Studio 2022 supports libFuzzer directly: 1. A new console project `fuzz_level` containing the target and the parser's source. 2. **C/C++ → Command Line**: `/fsanitize=fuzzer /fsanitize=address` (ASan makes memory bugs crash immediately instead of silently). 3. A `corpus` folder with a few valid level files as starting points. 4. Run: `fuzz_level.exe corpus -max_total_time=600` The fuzzer prints progress (`cov:` grows as it discovers code). On a crash it stops, prints the sanitizer report, and writes the input to a file such as `crash-3f2a...`. Running `fuzz_level.exe crash-3f2a...` reproduces it under the debugger. ## Minimising Fuzzer-found inputs are often large and noisy. **Minimisation** shrinks one to the smallest input that still fails, which usually makes the bug obvious. libFuzzer does it with `-minimize_crash=1`; the underlying idea is simple enough to write yourself, and the practice task does: repeatedly try removing parts of the input, keeping any removal after which it still fails. ## Fuzzing a driver's interface Lesson 16.10's test plan included fuzzing the driver from user mode: a program in the lab VM that opens the device and sends random control codes, lengths and buffer contents in a loop, with Driver Verifier on. Any bug check is a finding; the last request is logged before sending, so it can be reproduced. That is exactly how many real driver vulnerabilities are found, which is why driver authors should do it first. ## Common mistakes > [!warning] Fuzzing without sanitizers > Most memory bugs do not crash on their own. Combine fuzzing with ASan. > [!warning] Slow targets > A target doing file I/O or logging runs a hundred times slower and finds far less. > [!warning] Fixing the crash but not adding the input to the tests > Every fuzzer finding becomes a regression test (lesson 17.01). ## Knowledge check ```quiz ? What makes a coverage-guided fuzzer better than random inputs? + It keeps inputs that reach new code and mutates them further, gradually learning the input format - It uses a list of known bugs - It runs faster > New coverage guides the search. ? Why run a fuzz target with AddressSanitizer? + So memory errors that would not crash on their own are detected immediately - To make it faster - Fuzzers require it to compile > Silent overruns become clear failures. ? What does minimising a crashing input achieve? + The smallest input that still fails, which usually makes the cause obvious - A faster fuzzer - A fix for the bug > Then add it as a regression test. ```
ideas:
- Write a fuzz target for the INI parser from lesson 10.08's practice task, run it for ten minutes with ASan, and fix anything it finds.
- Write a target for the telemetry snapshot reader from lesson 12.04 with the invariant "encoding the decoded snapshot gives back the original bytes".
- Take a crash input and minimise it with `-minimize_crash=1`.

cards.q: What makes a good fuzz target?
cards.a: It passes the fuzzer's bytes to one parser or decoder of untrusted data, is fast and deterministic, checks invariants as well as crashes, and has no outside side effects.

cards.q: How do you run libFuzzer with MSVC?
cards.a: Compile the target with `/fsanitize=fuzzer` (and `/fsanitize=address`), then run the executable with a corpus folder and options such as a time limit.

cards.q: What should happen to every input a fuzzer finds?
cards.a: It should be minimised, used to fix the bug, and added to the test suite as a regression test.
